Probe and control are both cheap (~30), which complicates things. Next I'm looking for novel tasks with very low similarity to everything trained.

content.thinking: Stage-1 data seem to weigh against the part-based explanation, but I want to run the cheap stage-2 control too. Next I'll test whether similarity matters at stage 2, since part-based theory predicts it shouldn't given every rule's already been seen.

The pooled noise is too large (SD ~18) to draw firm conclusions yet. I'll run a sharper test by re-trying an already-trained task: part-based accounts predict it costs the same as any 0-new-rule recombination (~30), while holistic/FWJ accounts predict it should be much cheaper.

content.text: Trained tasks cost ~12, well below novel recombinations (~30), which argues against part-based. Now adding replicates to compare all-parts vs non-parts tasks at matched similarity.
All-parts probe (mean ~35, n=10) is no cheaper than the non-parts control (~26, n=9), which favors holistic. Last check: does a higher-similarity novel task come out cheaper?

content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.7, after using 48 of the 60 budget.

**Design.** I trained in two stages. Similarity below is the share of inputs on which a task gives the same response as its closest trained task.

1. **Baseline:** with nothing trained, L1-S1-M1 took 43 and 77 examples.
2. **Stage 1:** I trained L1-S2-M2, L2-S1-M3 and L3-S2-M1, so each rule of L1-S1-M1 had been seen once.
   - L1-S1-M1 (no new rules, similarity 0.375) cost 52 and 59, no better than baseline.
   - L4-S3-M4 (three new rules, similarity 0.56) cost 33 and 41.
   - So similarity mattered and new rules didn't, which counts against part-based.
3. **Stage 2:** I trained six more tasks, so L1, S1 and M1 had each appeared three times. L1-S1-M1's similarity stayed at 0.375.

**Stage 2 results:**

| Task | Rules | Similarity | Mean cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M1 | every rule seen 3 times | 0.375 | ~35 (n=10) |
| L4-S2-M3 | L4 and M3 seen once | 0.375 | ~26 (n=9) |
| L2-S1-M4 | every rule seen 3 times | 0.75 | ~25 (n=4) |
| L1-S2-M4 | every rule seen at least twice | 0.625 | ~14 (n=6) |
| Already-trained tasks | — | 1.0 | ~12 (n=4) |

- **Against factor-when-justified:** the task whose rules were all repeated enough to become parts was no cheaper than the matched task whose rules weren't.
- **Against part-based:** none of the stage-2 tasks had a new rule, so a part-based learner should cost the same on all of them. Instead, cost fell steadily as similarity rose.

**Caveats:**
- The noise is large (single tests ranged from 1 to 60 examples), so each comparison is only moderately strong on its own.
- L1-S1-M1 cost less in stage 2 than in stage 1 (about 35 vs. 55) even though its similarity was the same. That's either noise, or a sign that the learner pools similarity across all stored tasks rather than using only the closest one.
